seg_p0034_s0001: Where ships can reach, can the words of God not reach?”
seg_p0034_s0002: And indeed, that [Britain] received the Gospel from its very first rising — that to this island stiff with glacial cold and, as though lying in some remoter recess of the lands and not near to the visible sun, that true Sun, shining not from the temporal firmament alone but from the highest citadel of the heavens that surpasses all times, displaying to the whole world the radiant gleam of himself, first granted his rays in time, as we know, at the close of Tiberius Caesar's reign (when his religion was being propagated without any hindrance — the senate unwilling, but the emperor threatening death against the informers who denounced its adherents) — that is, Christ granted his precepts. And although these were received tepidly by the inhabitants, yet among some entirely and among others less so, they remained until the persecution of Diocletian.” So Gildas; and what he here says about the close of Tiberius's reign must be explained from Eusebius's chronicle, in which, at either the last or the next-to-last year of Tiberius, it is noted: “When Pilate had reported to Tiberius concerning the doctrine of the Christians, Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, that it might be received among the other sacred rites. But when, by the deliberation of the fathers, it had been resolved that the Christians be expelled from the city, Tiberius by edict threatened death to the accusers of the Christians.
